supplement.where: Appendix 1: AI augmented ideation tool, PDF pp. 28-29 (printed pp. xxvi-xxvii), referenced in Section 4.1 on PDF p. 13. No external supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Four screenshots of the tool overview, persona generation, persona contributions, and task-solution input. No additional outcome statistics, SDs, SEs, or confidence intervals are supplied in this appendix.

paper_design_summary: Students at the University of Regensburg were randomly assigned to AI-assisted or no-AI conditions and then worked in teams on healthcare and automotive innovation proposals; the reported sample comprises 70 students, 24 teams, and 48 ideas (PDF pp. 12-14, Sections 4-4.1). The AI condition used a custom GPT-4 Turbo tool with conversational expert personas, and both conditions completed the same timed tasks (PDF p. 4, Section 1; pp. 13-14, Section 4.1). Blinded experts scored proposal quality, and Task 1 ideas were also classified by innovation type; these are assisted-production outcomes from one experiment, not an AI-output-versus-human-output comparison or an AI-withdrawal study (PDF pp. 12, 15, 17, 20, Sections 4-5).

studies.label: Randomized student-team ideation experiment: elderly healthcare and automotive business models

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly assigned to the experimental or control condition and then organized into teams. The experimental condition received the custom GenAI tool; control received no AI. The same condition applied to both tasks. The randomization procedure and allocation ratio are not stated.
assignment.quote: In the first phase, participants are randomly assigned to either an experimental group or a control group.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 12 (printed p. 10), Section 4, experimental phases; corroborated on PDF p. 4 (printed p. 2), Section 1, and p. 25 (printed p. 23), Section 7.

arms.name: GenAI-assisted team ideation
arms.description: Teams received an introduction and Q&A about the custom GenAI tool, then used it to develop and submit consensus solutions to both tasks. The tool generated and conversed through tailored AI expert personas (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 4.1).

arms.name: Team ideation without AI
arms.description: Teams brainstormed without AI after a brief introduction, using the same tasks and background information, and submitted through Google Forms; they worked in a separate room and were not told that the experimental condition used AI (PDF pp. 12-15, Sections 4-4.2).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions, withdrawals, or participant-flow accounting are stated. The analyzed count uses the paper's reported study sample of 70 students associated with the 48 generated ideas; it is not a separately reported count at randomization. Counts by arm are absent. The description of three-person teams is not reconciled with 70 students in 24 teams (PDF pp. 12-14, Sections 4-4.1).
participants.who: University of Regensburg business, economics, and information systems students with coursework in International Management and Strategic Management; they had limited exposure to healthcare and automotive innovation (PDF pp. 13-14, Section 4.1). The country is not expressly stated in the participant description.
participants.quote: The study involved 70 students in 24 teams, generating 48 unique ideas.
participants.locator: PDF p. 14 (printed p. 12), Section 4.1, participant and sample paragraphs; University of Regensburg identified on PDF p. 13 (printed p. 11).

ai_tool.name_model: Custom GenAI-assisted creativity support system based on OpenAI GPT-4 Turbo (PDF p. 4, Section 1); methods also call the backend GPT-4 (PDF p. 13, Section 4.1).
ai_tool.how_used: Teams entered a problem and conversed with four AI expert personas tailored to that problem, receiving ideas, insights, and feedback; revised problem descriptions could regenerate the personas. Automated prompts reused the conversation transcript. Teams submitted solutions through the interface once consensus was reached. The stated temperature setting was zero (PDF p. 13, Section 4.1; interface screenshots on PDF pp. 28-29, Appendix 1).

task.description: Each team produced a concrete solution proposal for each of two tasks: a product/service innovation in healthcare for seniors and an automotive business-model innovation considering autonomous driving. The two tasks used the same participant sample and conditions (PDF p. 12, Section 4).
task.duration: Maximum 45 minutes per task, with earlier submission permitted (PDF p. 14, Section 4.1).

outcomes.name: Aggregated idea-quality score
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Aggregate of the expert-rated Dean et al. idea-quality dimensions; the aggregation formula and weights are not specified. This is the main overall score discussed under H1, but no outcome is explicitly designated primary. Blinded domain-expert panel rated team solution proposals using the Dean et al. framework on a 7-point Likert scale (PDF p. 12, Section 4, and p. 15, Section 4.2). The analysis compares mean quality scores per idea; the two tasks are combined (PDF p. 15, Sections 4.2-5). The reported corpus contains 48 ideas (PDF p. 14, Section 4.1); no outcome-specific omissions are stated. Figures 2-3 show distributions and arm means, Figure 4 shows p-values from 1000 bootstrap variations, and Figure 5 plots Cohen's d (PDF pp. 16-20). These are analyses of the same outcome. Numerical SDs, SEs, confidence intervals, and exact numerical Cohen's d values are not printed; Figure 3 has error bars without a stated definition. No adjustment for repeated ideas from the same team is described. Table 3 labels its coefficient column t-test, but the accompanying text identifies those entries as regression coefficients (PDF pp. 18-19).

contrasts.reported: Mean: Experimental (E) 4.583, Control (C) 3.546. Table 2: t = -4.450938, p = 0.000056. Table 3: coefficient (column headed t-test) = 1.037037, p = 0.000054, R-squared = 0.301027. No numerical SD, SE, or confidence interval is reported. Cohen's d is plotted without numerical bar labels in Figure 5. The accompanying prose states Cohen's d above 0.8 for this outcome (PDF p. 20).

outcomes.name: Revolutionary innovation classification
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Indicator that an idea was classified as revolutionary under the Abernathy and Clark innovation matrix. The panel classified ideas by their impact on existing technological competencies and market relationships (PDF p. 8, Section 2.2; p. 12, Section 4; p. 15, Section 4.2). Only Task 1 ideas were included in the innovation-type analysis because the predefined autonomous-driving problem in Task 2 could bias classification (PDF p. 17, Section 5; p. 20, Section 5). A point-biserial correlation relates AI assistance to each category. The four categories are recorded as separate reported indicators of one nominal classification; they are not a measure of diversity across teams or an ordered creativity scale. No category counts or percentages, or explicit number of ideas analyzed for this task-specific test, are printed.

contrasts.reported: Task 1, revolutionary innovation: point-biserial r = 0.275, p = 0.193. The paper states that none of the innovation-type correlations was statistically significant.

company_involvement.description: No company funding, company author affiliation, or company participation in conducting the study is stated. The authors list University Regensburg, describe a tool developed for the study, and acknowledge academic and personal support. Use of OpenAI technology is reported but does not establish company involvement in the research.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1, author affiliations; p. 13, Section 4.1; p. 40 (printed p. xxxviii), Acknowledgements.

eligibility.reason: Random assignment of people to GenAI assistance versus no AI is explicit (PDF p. 12, Section 4). The reported study sample is 70 students, distinct from its 24 teams and 48 ideas, satisfying the people threshold; no exclusions are reported, although the participant flow and per-arm counts are not supplied (PDF p. 14, Section 4.1). Blinded experts scored the actual team proposals, including originality and aggregate idea quality, on a 7-point scale (PDF pp. 12 and 15, Sections 4 and 4.2; results in PDF p. 18, Tables 2-3). AI was available during production (PDF pp. 12-14). Under the codebook, the dedicated timed sessions in separate rooms/stations are coded lab_rct; the authors call the study a controlled/framed field experiment, but do not establish that the tasks were ordinary coursework (PDF pp. 13-14).

one_line_finding: AI-assisted teams produced ideas with higher aggregate expert-rated quality (4.583 versus 3.546; t = -4.450938, p = 0.000056; PDF pp. 16-18, Section 5, Figure 3 and Table 2).
open_questions: The paper reports 70 students in 24 teams but also describes three-person teams; the actual team sizes, initial randomized count, per-arm people counts, and exclusions are not documented (PDF pp. 12-14, Sections 4-4.1).

The two ideas contributed by each team are combined in the main quality analysis, but no team-clustered SE, participant-level analysis, or mixed model is described. Independent-unit precision would be needed before pooling (PDF pp. 12, 15, 18-20, Sections 4-5).

Numerical SDs/SEs/confidence intervals and exact Cohen's d values are unavailable in this PDF; the definition of Figure 3 error bars and the bootstrap resampling unit are also unstated (PDF pp. 17-20, Figures 3-5 and Tables 2-3).

Confirm the classification of the sessions as lab versus ordinary-coursework field research if additional documentation is obtained; the paper's own field-experiment label differs from the dedicated-session setting described (PDF pp. 12-14).
notes: Screened on 2026-10-09. Locators use physical PDF page numbers; the main-text printed page number is two less. The entire markdown conversion, including references, appendix, acknowledgements, and AI-writing declaration, was read. All recorded numerical results were checked against PDF page text; all figures and appendix screenshots were also inspected. Only this B form was opened/written under forms. Outcome inventory: Tables 2-3 and Figures 2-5 contain the aggregate quality score and nine component ratings. The four innovation-type indicators reported on PDF p. 20 are additionally listed, with the H5 revolutionary indicator first; there are fourteen recorded outcomes and no outcomes omitted because of the form cap. The task-specific quality descriptions on PDF p. 15, t-tests, regressions, bootstrap checks, and Cohen's d plots are treated as analyses of the same ten quality outcomes. The two tasks are not separate studies. The fifteen participants across three usability studies used to refine the tool are development work without reported comparative creativity outcomes, not additional eligible experiments or members added to the main sample (PDF p. 13, Section 4.1). Despite the word diversity in the abstract and H4, H4 is operationalized through originality, paradigm relevance, and feasibility ratings of individual ideas (PDF p. 11, Table 1; pp. 14-15, Section 4.2). No semantic similarity, lexical overlap, across-team dispersion, or other direct across_people diversity statistic is reported. Innovation-type classification tests category membership, not the diversity of a set. The later expert-evaluation phase scores the same assisted outputs and is not an after_ai task. Other reported measures are task-completion time, quality/time efficiency, and self-reported satisfaction/engagement (PDF p. 11, Table 1, H2-H3 and H6; pp. 17 and 21, Section 5); these are not output-scored creativity/diversity outcomes. The claim of more idea output per unit time on PDF p. 21 is not accompanied by a distinct reported fluency comparison. The main tables contain means, t statistics, p-values, coefficients, and R-squared but no numerical SDs or SEs; therefore arm_means_sds_ns and regression_coefficient_se are not marked available. standardized_effect and figure_only denote the plotted Cohen's d values, whose exact magnitudes have not been estimated from bar heights. No effect sizes or SEs were computed. Table 2 negative t statistics are preserved as printed alongside the higher experimental means and positive regression coefficients. The broad claim that every mean difference is significant on PDF pp. 16-17 is contradicted for applicability by Table 2 and by the conclusion on PDF p. 26; its contrast is coded no_clear_difference. The prose on PDF p. 20 calls paradigm-relatedness and acceptability medium effects, whereas their Figure 5 bars exceed its large-effect reference line; no exact d values are inferred. No preregistration, external statistical supplement, study data URL, or study code URL is supplied in the PDF. The source date is the date printed on the cover, not an inferred arXiv upload or revision date.
